extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, students, and readers of evolutionary biology and animal natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and diagnostic signs used to judge whether a given trait in animals has been produced by sexual selection (versus other causes), with special attention to lower animal classes (Mollusca, Crustacea, Arachnida, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of secondary sexual characters where sexes united or immobile
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary sexual characters (of the kind under consideration) do not occur in classes or sub-kingdoms where the two sexes are united in the same individual or where individuals are permanently attached to a support, or where mental powers are too low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sexes are hermaphroditic, permanently affixed, or have 'too imperfect senses and much too low mental powers to appreciate each other’s beauty or other attractions, or to feel rivalry,' sexual selection is unlikely to have produced conspicuous sexual ornaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex-specific conspicuous coloration as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: There is sufficient evidence that colours have been acquired by sexual selection only when one sex is much more brilliantly or conspicuously coloured than the other, and where no difference in habits between the sexes can account for the colour difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that the conspicuousness be sex-biased and not explained by differing exposures or habits; otherwise coloration may be non-sexual in origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary display to the opposite sex
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence is rendered most complete when the more ornamented individuals (almost always the males) voluntarily display their attractions before the other sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation of voluntary display behavior strongly supports sexual selection, because display would be purposeless unless it served to attract or excite the opposite sex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait appears at sexual maturity (ontogenetic timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual characters that are acquired only when the individual becomes mature and nearly ready to breed are eminently distinctive of characters acquired through sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a trait emerges at or just before reproductive maturity (and is absent in juveniles), that timing favors a sexual-selection explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex-biased enhancement of sensory organs for finding mates
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater development of sensory structures in one sex (e.g., males having more numerous olfactory threads on antennae) suggests selection for ability to find mates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare sexes: an increase in smell/antennae/sensory structures in the searching sex is consistent with sexual selection for mate-locating efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural adaptations for securing/holding mates
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifications such as prehensile antennae, enlarged chelae (pincers), and hook-like processes used to seize or hold the female indicate selection for mating success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When morphological differences clearly serve to grasp or hold females during reproduction (e.g., modified antennae or enlarged chelae used in pairing), sexual selection is a plausible cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male dimorphism and alternative mating forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of two or more distinct male forms (dimorphism) specialized for different mating tasks (e.g., one form with enhanced smelling-threads, another with enlarged chelae) indicates sexual selection acting on different successful strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If distinct male morphs each provide mating advantages (finding vs. holding females) and do not grade into one another, sexual selection and frequency-dependent advantages are likely explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male-biased size and weaponry as sign of male–male competition
rubrics_metrics.description: When the male is larger than the female and bears enlarged weapon-like structures (chelae, claws), this often reflects past male–male fighting and sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large male size and weapons that can be used in combat support an interpretation of intrasexual competition; corroborating behavioral evidence strengthens the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observed male aggression or lethal interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct observations of males fighting, mutilating, or displacing rivals (including experimental or captive observations) indicate sexual selection via competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports of males mutilating/killing one another, displacing paired males, or clear agonistic interactions are direct behavioral evidence for competition-driven sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing, guarding, and carrying behaviors support sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Behaviors such as males carrying the female, closing or guarding the burrow mouth, or otherwise guarding mates are consistent with sexual selection pressures (mate guarding/assurance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral accounts where males secure or guard females (e.g., carrying shell of female hermit crab, closing burrow with a large chela) support adaptive explanations tied to mating success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative (non-sexual) explanations must be excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Bright colours or conspicuous traits may result from protection (camouflage, warning coloration), physical/chemical tissue properties, or habitat-related exposure rather than sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before attributing ornamentation to sexual selection, consider and rule out other functions: protection (transparency, warning), physiological by-products (biliary glands), or environmental effects (light exposure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit-based explanations as an anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in colour or form between sexes that track differences in habits (e.g., one sex wandering and being more exposed to light) are likely due to habit, not sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether different lifestyles or exposures of the sexes can account for morphological differences; if so, sexual selection is a less parsimonious explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hermaphrodite ornamentation generally not sexual-selection driven
rubrics_metrics.description: In hermaphroditic species that pair, sexual selection is improbable because both individuals produce gametes; ornamentation is more likely to be due to natural selection unless pairing involves choosiness that confers advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For hermaphrodites, consider whether beauty correlates with vigour and confers differential reproductive success; otherwise, natural selection is the more likely driver.
